Sporting goods retail in France: 27 years of monthly demand

Stationarity, decomposition, drift, anomaly detection and forecast benchmarking on public INSEE data

Théophile L. Mouton

2026-11-18

Table of contents

  • Why this analysis
  • 1. Stationarity
  • 2. Decomposition
  • 3. Anomaly detection
  • 4. Drift
  • 5. Forecast benchmarking
  • 6. Forecast to August 2027
  • Limitations and next steps
  • Reproducibility

Key findings

  • Growth has stalled. The trend grew by 4.7 % a year between 2000 and 2019, but only 0.8 % a year between 2022 and 2025, in current euros, so likely a decline in volume once inflation is accounted for.
  • Seasonality is drifting. August now sits 36 % above trend (versus 30 % in 2010-2019), December has weakened, and the November trough has become shallower.
  • Covid breaks naive pipelines. Robust anomaly detection flags the lockdowns (April 2020: -78 % versus expected). Neutralising them cuts the ETS 12-month error from 7.9 % to 3.0 %.
  • The simplest model wins on a flat market. In a rolling backtest, the seasonal naive benchmark (2.4 % MAPE) beats ETS, ARIMA and Theta.

Why this analysis

Demand forecasting in retail starts with understanding the series: is it stationary, how strong and how stable is the seasonality, which observations are anomalies, and has the process drifted? Product-level sales are confidential, but INSEE publishes a monthly turnover index for retail sale of sporting equipment in specialised stores (NAF rev. 2 class 47.64). It covers January 1999 to August 2026, which makes it a good public testbed for the full workflow: stationarity tests, decomposition, anomaly detection, drift detection and honest forecast evaluation.

The index is in value (turnover, current euros), unadjusted, base 2021 = 100. All modelling is done on the log scale.

Show code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(df.index, df["brut"], color=GREY, lw=1, label="Monthly turnover index")
ax.plot(tr.index, tr, color=SURF, lw=2.5, label="Trend (robust STL)")
a = anom[covid_mask]
ax.scatter(a.index, np.exp(a["obs"]), s=40, color=ORANGE, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5, zorder=5,
           label="Covid anomalies")
ax.set_ylabel("Index (2021 = 100)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()

1. Stationarity

The augmented Dickey-Fuller test (null hypothesis: unit root) and the KPSS test (null hypothesis: stationarity) are complementary, so they are read together.

Show code 
stat.style.format("{:.3f}")

The log level is non-stationary (ADF does not reject a unit root, KPSS rejects stationarity). After first or seasonal differencing both tests agree on stationarity. This points to a stochastic trend plus a strong annual cycle: models need either differencing (ARIMA) or an explicit trend and seasonal state (ETS).

2. Decomposition

A robust STL decomposition (period 12) separates trend, seasonality and remainder. The robust weights stop the Covid months from distorting the trend and seasonal estimates.

Show code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(9, 8), sharex=True)
for ax, col, lab, c in zip(axes, ["obs", "trend", "seasonal", "resid"],
                           ["Observed (log)", "Trend", "Seasonal", "Remainder"],
                           [GREY, SURF, MID, DEEP]):
    if col == "resid":
        ax.bar(dec.index, dec[col], width=25, color=c)
    else:
        ax.plot(dec.index, dec[col], color=c, lw=1.5)
    ax.set_ylabel(lab, fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

3. Anomaly detection

Anomalies are flagged on the STL remainder using a robust z-score (median and MAD rather than mean and standard deviation), with a threshold of |z| > 3.5. A robust scale matters here: a few extreme Covid months would otherwise inflate the standard deviation and hide everything else.

Show code 
out = anom[["z", "vs_expected_pct"]].copy()
out.index = out.index.strftime("%Y-%m")
out.columns = ["Robust z-score", "Deviation from expected (%)"]
out.style.format("{:.1f}")

The Covid lockdowns dominate (March-April 2020, November 2020, April 2021), followed by catch-up months that are just as anomalous in the other direction. Isolated pre-Covid flags are much smaller (mostly under 10 %) and plausibly linked to weather, calendar or promotional effects.

4. Drift

Trend

Show code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
gg = (np.exp(g) - 1) * 100
ax.plot(gg.index, gg, color=SURF, lw=2)
ax.axhline(0, color=INK2, lw=0.8)
for b in breaks:
    ax.axvline(b, color=ORANGE, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set_ylabel("Trend growth, year on year (%)")
plt.show()

Change-point detection (PELT, RBF cost) on the year-on-year trend growth finds breaks at 2001-03, 2004-02, 2007-11, 2014-07, 2019-12, 2021-03, 2023-04. The last regime, since 2023, is a plateau: 0.8 % a year against 4.7 % on average before Covid.

Seasonality

Show code 
months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
x = np.arange(12)
w = 0.27
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i, (col, c) in enumerate(zip(prof.columns, [FOAM, LIGHT, SURF])):
    ax.bar(x + (i - 1) * w, prof[col], w * 0.95, color=c, label=col)
ax.axhline(0, color=INK2, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xticks(x, months)
ax.set_ylabel("Deviation from trend (%)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()
Show code 
t = prof.copy()
t.index = months
t.T.style.format("{:+.0f}")

The seasonal pattern is not fixed. Back-to-school and summer (August) has grown, while December has lost weight, and November has become less of a trough. Black Friday shifting spend from December to November is a plausible explanation, though it is not tested here. For a forecasting pipeline this means seasonal factors estimated on long histories will be biased, and models that let seasonality evolve, or that weight recent years, should be preferred.

5. Forecast benchmarking

Four models from statsforecast are compared in a rolling-origin backtest: 12-month horizon, three origins (2023-08, 2024-08, 2025-08), each refit on all data available at the origin. Each model is run on the raw series and on a version where March 2020 to May 2021 is replaced by the STL trend plus seasonal estimate.

Show code 
order = ["Seasonal naive", "ETS", "ARIMA", "Theta"]
yy = np.arange(4)[::-1]
h = 0.38
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.barh(yy + h / 2, btr.loc[order, "MAPE (%)"], h * 0.95, color=GREY, label="Raw data")
ax.barh(yy - h / 2, btc.loc[order, "MAPE (%)"], h * 0.95, color=SURF, label="Covid neutralised")
for yi, v in zip(yy, btr.loc[order, "MAPE (%)"]):
    ax.text(v + 0.1, yi + h / 2, f"{v:.1f}", va="center", fontsize=10, color=INK2)
for yi, v in zip(yy, btc.loc[order, "MAPE (%)"]):
    ax.text(v + 0.1, yi - h / 2, f"{v:.1f}", va="center", fontsize=10)
ax.set_yticks(yy, order)
ax.set_xlabel("MAPE (%)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()
Show code 
bt.style.format({"MAPE (%)": "{:.2f}", "Bias (%)": "{:+.2f}", "80% interval coverage (%)": "{:.0f}"}).hide(axis="index")

Three lessons:

  1. Cleaning the Covid period matters more than the choice of model. On raw data, ETS over-forecasts by about 6 %, most likely because it reads the 2020-2022 rebound as trend. Neutralising those months cuts its error by a factor of 2.6.
  2. On a flat market, seasonal naive is hard to beat. Once growth stops and seasonality is stable year to year, repeating last year is a strong forecast. Any production model should be benchmarked against it.
  3. Check calibration, not just accuracy. Theta’s 80 % intervals cover only 72 % of outcomes, so it is overconfident. Stock decisions depend on the interval, not the point forecast.

6. Forecast to August 2027

hist = df.loc["2022-01-01":, "brut"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(hist.index, hist, color=INK2, lw=1.8, label="Observed")

ax.fill_between(fc["ds"], fc[f"{best_key}-lo-80"], fc[f"{best_key}-hi-80"], color=LIGHT, label="80 % interval")
ax.plot(fc["ds"], fc[best_key], color=SURF, lw=2.5, label=f"Forecast ({best.lower()})")

ax.legend(loc="upper left")

The December 2026 peak is expected at 140 (80 % interval 128 to 154).

Limitations and next steps

  • Aggregate, value-based series. This is a national turnover index, not unit sales by product and store. Inflation is mixed with volume, and the hierarchical, intermittent and promotion-driven structure of real assortment data is absent.
  • Short backtest. Three yearly origins give 36 forecast points. Results are indicative, not a definitive model ranking.
  • Covid neutralisation uses the full-sample STL fit. The imputed months lie before all backtest origins, so leakage is minimal, but a strictly causal version would refit STL at each origin.
  • Next steps: exogenous drivers (weather, calendar, Black Friday and Olympics dummies), a deflated volume series, and zero-shot time series foundation models (Chronos, TimesFM) compared against the same seasonal naive baseline.

Reproducibility

Data: INSEE, Indice de chiffre d’affaires - Commerce de détail d’articles de sport en magasin spécialisé (NAF rév. 2, 47.64), series 010770520 (raw) and 010770580 (seasonally and calendar adjusted), retrieved from the INSEE BDM SDMX API. scripts/fetch_insee.py refreshes the data, and quarto render report.qmd rebuilds this page.
